cases.description: An empty operation sequence is a valid request with no per-operation results.
Empty requests, initial report, and zero-event audit.
Issuing an invoice changes receivables but no cash.
A partial payment produces partial status and balanced reconciliation.
Allocation input order is preserved in audit while report rows sort by ID.
An exactly settled invoice is paid.
Separate payments accumulate on one invoice.
Rejected duplicate ID consumes neither its request key nor an event ID.
One missing invoice rejects the whole allocation list and leaves the key reusable.
A later overpayment must roll back an earlier valid allocation.
Invoice and payment retries return their original IDs without changing audit.
Keys conflict across mutation kinds and changed payloads.
Reordering allocation entries is a conflicting payload, while object field order is irrelevant.
New writes into a closed period fail; an accepted earlier payload replays; later-period writes work.
Closing is monotonic; future events do not block closing an earlier period, and open-period backdating works.
Reports and audits use event prefixes including close events, not posting-period ordering.
Future prefixes and malformed prefixes produce distinct read errors without consuming sequence IDs.
Validate bounds, types, identifiers, unknown fields, duplicate allocations, and operation structure before touching state.
Structural validation precedes retry; key conflict precedes closed-period checks; missing invoice precedes overpayment.
Aggregate cash can exceed 32-bit integer range and must remain exact.
Reject malformed task input before executing operations.
Reject malformed task input before executing operations.
Reject malformed task input before executing operations.
Returning part of a settled payment reopens the invoice without reducing its billed total.
A fully returned payment leaves an unpaid invoice with its original total.
A refund is limited by payment allocation, not invoice total, and may exhaust a partial payment.
Multiple partial refunds accumulate and a one-unit excess is rejected.
Refund only selected original allocations; untouched invoices retain their balances.
A refund exceeding one original allocation rejects the whole event and permits corrected reuse of the key.
An existing invoice funded by a different payment cannot be refunded against this payment.
Refunds consume capacity on their named payment, even with several payments on the invoice.
Refund retries do not return money twice; changed amount conflicts without a new event.
Refund targets distinguish missing events from nonpayment events; failures leave the key available.
Payment reversal reopens all its allocations and appends compensation without rewriting the original.
One reversal removes every allocation from its target payment.
Reversing a refund restores paid status and removes active refunded totals.
A payment with an active refund cannot be reversed; rejecting it preserves all accounting state.
Reversing all refunds removes the payment-reversal block; a failed reversal key can be reused.
After reversing a refund, its amount can be refunded again against the same payment.
A replacement payment can prevent reversal of a refund; the failure is atomic and does not reserve the key.
A blocked restoration on the later invoice must not partially restore the earlier invoice.
Cannot reverse invoices, close events, unknown events, or another reversal.
Retry the same reversal key successfully; a different key targeting the reversed event fails.
A reversed payment remains in audit but cannot fund a refund; replaying it does not reactivate it.
Replaying an old refund after its reversal returns its original receipt without changing restored money.
New refund and reversal entries need open posting periods, but can correct events from closed periods.
An already accepted refund or reversal replays after its posting period closes; changed payload conflicts first.
Every event prefix retains its original balances, refund totals, and immutable audit history.
Malformed extension operations consume no IDs or keys, including duplicate allocation invoices and invalid event references.
An allocation outside the target wins over excessive capacity; closed-period validation wins over missing target.
Returning money permits a replacement payment but does not enlarge the original payment refund capacity.
An interleaved correction workflow preserves independent allocations, retry keys after rejection, closed periods, old snapshots, and complete audit order.
Reject 501 operations at input validation rather than producing partial read results.
Reversing one refund restores only its target payment capacity; another fully refunded payment stays exhausted.
Repeated payment/refund cycles can produce active refunded totals above the billed total; reversing one cycle can block reversal of another.
